Mocking the Integration Test

The same technique, one layer higher: a real Express app, still with no real database underneath it.

Lesson 1's endpoint test (Figure 1.15) sent real HTTP-shaped requests into the exported app via Supertest — genuinely exercising routing and middleware, not calling a function directly. That's still true here; only what's underneath has changed:

// Figure 2.20: mocking one layer higher (tests/integration/tickets.routes.test.js, excerpt)
jest.unstable_mockModule('../../src/config/db.js', () => ({
  default: mockPrisma,
}));

const { default: app } = await import('../../src/app.js');

it('POST /tickets without a customerId returns 400', async () => {
  const res = await request(app)
    .post('/tickets')
    .send({ subject: 'Cannot reset password', description: 'Link expired' });

  expect(res.status).toBe(400);
  expect(mockPrisma.ticket.create).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
});

Exactly the same jest.unstable_mockModule() + dynamic import() pattern as the unit test — just importing app.js afterward instead of ticket.service.js directly. app.js imports routes, which import controllers, which import ticket.service.js, which imports db.js (Figure 2.14's whole chain) — mocking db.js before any of that chain loads means the entire request — real Express routing, the real controller's validation, the real service's Prisma calls — runs for real, right up until the one point it would have actually touched a database.

The last assertion is worth noticing on its own: expect(mockPrisma.ticket.create).not.toHaveBeenCalled() confirms the request was rejected by the controller's customerId check (the previous topic) before it ever reached Prisma — proof the validation actually short-circuits the database call, not just that a 400 came back.
